title: AI Game Dev Pop Dynasty
author: Fun_Tumbleweed_3682
selftext:
Hello! I am the developer of \*Pop Dynasty\*, an idle management simulation game where you run an entertainment agency. You can currently play a free demo version on Steam:



Steam (Play the demo and add to your wishlist):

[https://store.steampowered.com/app/5579680/Pop\_Dynasty\_Demo/?beta=0](https://store.steampowered.com/app/5579680/Pop_Dynasty_Demo/?beta=0)



Trailer Video:





Core Gameplay Loop



\- Recruit pop stars, each with their own unique talents and traits.

\- Assign your pop stars to various activities: improve their stats through training, boost their charm at the clinic, and generate revenue and fame through different engagements. Send them on tours to earn significant profits—and perhaps even discover new equipment along the way.

\- Utilize facilities and advertising campaigns to enhance your agency as a whole or boost the capabilities of individual pop stars.

\- Your agency continues to operate even when you’re not playing.

\- Build your team and compete in awards shows. Each event consists of multiple rounds—covering categories like talent, charm, and fame, as well as special rounds such as "Ace Showdown" or "Team Harmony"—where you must win a majority of the rounds to claim overall victory.

\- Winning an awards show for the first time earns you a trophy; collecting more trophies makes your entire agency even more powerful.



Demo Version Content



\- The start of the first "Generation": Includes 10 pop stars and 3 awards shows, offering approximately 30 minutes of gameplay.

\- Higher-tier trainers, tours, and clinics are currently locked, but you can view them as blurred-out previews. - In the demo version, rewards for offline progress accumulate for a maximum of 1 hour (in the full version, they can accumulate for up to 12 hours).

\- Play data from the demo version cannot be transferred to the full version.



Full Version Content



\- Features 200 pop stars, 150 awards ceremonies, trainers across 8 different fields, and 30 types of activities.

\- Winning the "Generation Finale" triggers the start of a new generation. While I’ll keep the details of what carries over to the next generation a secret, some names will certainly never be forgotten.



Supported Platforms: Windows.

Supported Languages: English, Korean, Japanese, Chinese (Simplified/Traditional), Spanish (Latin American), and Portuguese (Brazilian).



I would love to hear your feedback on the game’s overall structure, style, and pacing. I am currently generating images for the pop stars in the full version and am open to suggestions for improvement.



Disclosure of AI Usage



\- Code: Written by me, with AI used for recommendations and review.

\- Graphics: AI was used to create in-game characters and assets, which I then personally reviewed.

\- Text: AI was used for translation.

\- Sound: AI was used for generation, followed by my own manual review.



I relied on AI for code review, while handling the review of other elements personally. Is it possible to clearly distinguish between human review and AI review in your experience?



Personally, I feel uneasy if I don’t review everything myself, so I even built a dedicated web page to facilitate my own manual review process.



What kind of workflow do you use?

comments.author: No-Volume6352
comments.body:
The direction is completely different, but I'm a solo developer currently working on an anime-style rhythm game, so this caught my interest.

You mentioned you write the code yourself—so are you more on the engineering side?
Do you feel less confident with areas like art, music, and UI/UX?

Setting aside the "AI-ness" that's very apparent for now, here are some observations from what I can see:

**The importance of having your own art style**  
Since it's "pop and idol," this is only natural, but when you leave it to AI, you end up with vivid rainbow colors and sparkling gold scattered everywhere.

**Scope explosion**  
200 characters... Rather than thinly increasing the volume, I think a direction that deepens attractive characters would be better, but since it depends on the gameplay, I can't say for certain what the correct answer is. At the moment, it feels like they've become nothing more than symbols and numbers.

**Playing it**  
I actually tried the demo on Steam.
I enjoyed it more than I expected. I even cleared the demo.
The "idols" are just the visual presentation—the core is a game where you enjoy watching numbers go up.

Whether to take this in the direction of "The Idolmaster" or make it a Cookie Clicker wearing an idol skin—that feels like the difficult part of development.

replies.author: Fun_Tumbleweed_3682
replies.body:
Thank you very much for your comments.



To address your first question: I faced significant challenges in selecting the right design, sound, and UI/UX elements for the game. I relied on AI for assistance, reviewing each output and exploring alternative approaches where necessary.



While I am well aware that doing it all myself would be ideal, I found that no matter how much I studied or practiced, I couldn't achieve any meaningful improvement in the results—which is why I chose this approach.



Regarding the development of a unique art style, I experimented with various methods, including local AI models, GPT, and Gemini.



However, after two to three months of refining prompts for GPT and Gemini, I still couldn't eliminate that distinct, "artificial" quality. Consequently, I abandoned my original goal of a "semi-realistic" style and shifted toward an animation-inspired aesthetic.



For the "Pop Star" characters specifically, since GPT and Gemini couldn't produce the desired texture, I generated them locally and then manually post-edited each one (e.g., removing backgrounds).



I have many regrets, which I attribute to my own limitations; I am still actively exploring ways to generate the specific art style I envision using local AI models.



The 200 characters were originally intended for a "gacha" mechanic—similar to many mobile games—where players would pull for characters and then develop them.



The idea was to encourage players to seek out characters that shared their own nationality or MBTI type, but as the game’s development progressed, that mechanic no longer felt relevant, which is a bit of a shame.



As for the core gameplay, I drew inspiration from \*Melvor Idle\* and various other incremental games.



Although the demo lacks the "rebirth" (prestige) mechanic typical of the incremental genre, the full version will feature a similar system, along with cumulative progression mechanics, to align with that structure.
